title: Unicode vs UTF-8: what's the difference, with byte examples — cv.cm
description: Unicode assigns every character a number; UTF-8 turns that number into 1 to 4 bytes. See worked byte examples, UTF-16 and BOM, and why text turns into Ã©.
h1: What is the difference between Unicode and UTF-8?
answer: Unicode is a character set: it gives every character a number called a code point, such as U+00E9 for "é". UTF-8 is an encoding: a rule for storing those numbers as bytes. It uses 1 byte for ASCII and 2 to 4 bytes for everything else, so "é" becomes `C3 A9`. Unicode says which character; UTF-8 says how it is written to disk or sent over a network.

body: Unicode defines a code space from U+0000 to U+10FFFF, room for 1,114,112 code points split into 17 planes of 65,536 each. More than 150,000 of them are assigned to characters, covering modern and historic scripts, symbols and emoji. A code point is written as `U+` followed by at least four hex digits.

A code point is only a number. To save or transmit text, it has to be turned into bytes, and there are several ways to do that: UTF-8, UTF-16 and UTF-32 are all encodings of the same Unicode characters.

UTF-8, specified in RFC 3629, is a variable-width encoding. The leading bits of the first byte say how many bytes follow, and every continuation byte starts with the bits `10`. That makes the stream self-synchronizing: a decoder that lands in the middle of a character can skip forward to the next start byte.

Worked example: "é" is U+00E9, binary `000 1110 1001`. It needs the 2-byte pattern. The top 5 bits `00011` go into `110xxxxx` to give `11000011` (`C3`), and the low 6 bits `101001` go into `10xxxxxx` to give `10101001` (`A9`).

Because the first 128 code points encode to the same single bytes as ASCII, any valid ASCII file is already valid UTF-8. That backward compatibility is the main reason UTF-8 became the default for the web, where it is used by about 98% of websites.

body: UTF-16 stores characters above U+FFFF as a surrogate pair of two 16-bit units. That is why `"😀".length` is `2` in JavaScript: the language counts UTF-16 units, not characters. Iterating with `[..."😀"].length` returns `1`.
For English text UTF-8 is the most compact. For text that is mostly Chinese, Japanese or Korean, UTF-16 can be smaller, since those characters take 3 bytes in UTF-8 but 2 in UTF-16.

A BOM is the character U+FEFF placed at the very start of a file. In UTF-16 and UTF-32 it tells the reader whether the bytes are big-endian or little-endian. In UTF-8 it encodes as `EF BB BF` and serves only as a signature, since UTF-8 has no byte order.

The Unicode FAQ says a UTF-8 BOM is neither required nor recommended. Some Windows editors add it anyway, and it then breaks shell scripts (the `#!` line is no longer first), CSV headers and JSON parsers that do not expect it. If a file shows `ï»¿` at the top, that is a UTF-8 BOM read as Windows-1252.

sections.h: Why text turns into Ã© or ���
body: Garbled text, called mojibake, appears when bytes are decoded with a different encoding than the one used to write them:

ul: `Ã©` instead of `é`: UTF-8 bytes `C3 A9` read as Windows-1252 or Latin-1, which maps `C3` to `Ã` and `A9` to `©`.
`�` (U+FFFD, the replacement character): the decoder hit bytes that are not valid UTF-8, often Latin-1 text read as UTF-8.
Question marks in a database: the column or connection used a charset that cannot hold the character, so it was replaced on write and is gone.

body: The fix is to declare the encoding at every boundary: `<meta charset="utf-8">` in HTML, `Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8` in HTTP headers, and UTF-8 for database columns and connections. In MySQL, use `utf8mb4`; the older `utf8` charset stores at most 3 bytes per character and rejects emoji.

body.note: Mojibake caused by a wrong decode is reversible if you still have the original bytes. Text that was re-saved after being misread, or that lost characters to `?` on write, usually cannot be recovered.

faq.q: Is UTF-8 the same as Unicode?
faq.a: No. Unicode is the list of characters and their numbers; UTF-8 is one way to store those numbers as bytes. People often say "Unicode" when they mean UTF-8 text.

faq.q: How many bytes is a character in UTF-8?
faq.a: Between 1 and 4. ASCII letters take 1 byte, most European accented letters 2, most Chinese, Japanese and Korean characters 3, and emoji 4.
Yes. UTF-8 can encode every Unicode code point from U+0000 to U+10FFFF, so any character Unicode defines can be written in UTF-8.

faq.q: Should I save files with a BOM?
faq.a: For UTF-8, usually not. It is optional, adds nothing for byte order, and confuses tools that expect the first bytes to be content. Some older Excel versions need it to open UTF-8 CSV files correctly.
